Divorce, Cruelty & Court Procedure Judgments

Rulings on divorce for cruelty and desertion, irretrievable breakdown of marriage, arrest safeguards in matrimonial cases, and how family-court cases are run.

44 judgments · 16 from the Supreme Court · updated 25 November 2026

This page collects judgments on how family disputes are decided and run: divorce on grounds of cruelty and desertion, the Supreme Court’s power under Article 142 to dissolve a marriage that has irretrievably broken down, and when the six-month cooling-off period for mutual-consent divorce can be waived.

It also covers arrest safeguards in matrimonial cases (Arnesh Kumar and the cases enforcing it, including compensation and contempt for illegal arrests), jurisdiction, mediated settlements, evidence such as recorded calls, and directions to speed up family-court cases.

Judicial Reform Karnataka High Court
W.P. No. 26958 of 2026 (‘Parenting Time’ direction)
September 2026

Directed every Family Court in Karnataka to use ‘parenting time’ instead of ‘visitation’ in custody orders, because no parent is a mere visitor in a child’s life. In the case itself, brought by the mother, the Court stayed a 50:50 parenting plan pending hearing and fixed interim time for the father.

X v. X and Ors. (2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 448)
August 2026

Transferred a family court case to another court on a litigant’s apprehension of judicial bias, applying an objective ‘reasonable, fair-minded observer’ standard to preserve confidence in the process.

Judicial Reform Supreme Court
SC Upholds Wife’s Right to Husband’s Hotel & Call Records to Prove Adultery
July 2026

Directing production of hotel booking records and call detail records to establish adultery in a matrimonial case does not violate the right to privacy. The right to a fair trial and evidence permitted under Section 14 of the Family Courts Act can outweigh a spouse’s privacy claim — cuts toward disclosure obligations for whichever spouse is accused, not exclusively protective of either side.

PRECEDENT Read Report →
Judicial Reform Supreme Court
Gopalakrishna Surapaneni v. Anuradha Surpaneni Maiden (2026 INSC 623)
May 2026

Granted divorce under Article 142 after a 23-year separation, holding a marriage ‘dead for all practical purposes’ cannot be kept alive by court order — parties cannot be compelled to remain married once reconciliation is realistically impossible.

LANDMARK Read Full Judgment →
Judicial Reform Allahabad High Court
Sushma Devi v. State of U.P. — Lok Adalats Cannot Grant Divorce
April 30, 2026

Lok Adalats and DLSAs have no jurisdiction to grant divorce decrees — only Family Courts do. A ‘settlement’ recorded before a Lok Adalat does not dissolve a marriage in law; ruling directed to be circulated across UP after a husband tried to use one to justify remarrying with no valid divorce in place.

LANDMARK Full Judgment (PDF) →
Judicial Reform Supreme Court
Dhananjay Rathi v. Ruchika Rathi — Cannot Withdraw Consent After Settlement
April 13, 2026

Once parties enter a mediated settlement and act upon it, they are bound by its terms. A spouse cannot withdraw consent for mutual divorce after agreeing as part of a full and final settlement. Backtracking may attract serious costs.

Judicial Reform Madras High Court
Raj v. Inspector of Police — Trial Courts Cannot Impound Passport as a Bail Condition
April 6, 2026

A trial court cannot impose passport impoundment as a condition for granting bail.

Judicial Reform Supreme Court
Hamsaanandini Nanduri — Caregiving Equality
March 2026

The same bench that read down the adoptive-mother maternity-benefit age limit also urged Parliament to legislate paternity leave as a matter of caregiving equality, not just paternal goodwill. Parliament has not yet responded.

Judicial Reform Kerala High Court
Jinesh v. Aswathy — Adultery Standard of Proof in Maintenance Cases
November 19, 2025

A husband resisting maintenance on the ground that the wife is living in adultery (Section 125(4) CrPC / 144(4) BNSS) need prove it only on the preponderance of probability — the civil standard — not beyond reasonable doubt.

Anish Pramod Patel v. Kiran Jyot Maini
December 1, 2023

An accused cannot be summoned or arrested merely for non-payment of a monetary order under §31 of the DV Act — that provision does not create an independent criminal liability for default alone.

Judicial Reform Supreme Court
Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v. Union of India (2018) 10 SCC 443
Sept 2018

Reaffirmed the Arnesh Kumar arrest safeguards for 498A cases, but struck down mandatory ‘Family Welfare Committees’ to screen complaints before arrest as beyond the judiciary’s power — holding that such procedural filters must come from Parliament, not court-ordered guidelines.

Using these judgments

Official Court Copy opens the judgment PDF from the Supreme Court’s own website. Full Judgment opens the complete judgment text (Indian Kanoon, or a PDF copy of the order). Read Report opens a news or legal-blog summary where no full text is linked yet.

To rely on a judgment in court, cite it by its case number or citation; the court’s registry can issue a certified copy. Check that it has not been overturned or modified on appeal. The one-line summaries on this page are for information only and are not legal advice.
